name: Latgalian
variety: Standard Latgalian: the written standard of 2007 and the High Latvian varieties of Latgale (eastern Latvia) on which it rests. Treated in Latvia as a historical variety of Latvian and by many linguists as a separate language.
sources: Nau, Nicole (2011). A Short Grammar of Latgalian. München: Lincom Europa.
Leikuma, Lidija (2003). Latgalīšu volūda 1. Sanktpēterburga: Sanktpēterburgas Valsts universitāte.
Cibuļs, Juris & Leikuma, Lidija (2003). Vasals! Latgaliešu valodas mācība. Rīga: n.i.m.s.
Breidaks, Antons (2007). Darbu izlase. Rīga: LU Latviešu valodas institūts.
Balode, Laimute & Holvoet, Axel (2001). The Latvian language and its dialects. In Ö. Dahl & M. Koptjevskaja-Tamm (eds.), The Circum-Baltic Languages, vol. 1. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.
Laua, Alise (1997). Latviešu literārās valodas fonētika. Rīga: Zvaigzne ABC. (for the description of the syllable tones)
contrasts: palatalised versus plain consonants: consonants are soft before front vowels and the contrast is also found before back vowels and word-finally (soft final t of the infinitive, ļ, ņ, ķ, ģ)
central /ɨ/ (written y) after plain consonants versus /i/ after palatalised consonants; the two vowels are close to complementary distribution
phonemic vowel length (ā, ē, ī, ū; long ō is rare, y has no long partner in the standard spelling)
short /o/ as a native vowel (lobs, Latgola), where Latvian has /a/
narrow /e eː/ versus wide /æ æː/, both written e, ē
two syllable tones on long syllables: falling and broken
allophony: regular sound correspondences with Standard Latvian, reflected in the spelling: uo for Latvian ā (muote), ī for ie (dīna), ū for uo (ūtrys), ei for ī (dzeivs), iu or yu for ū (myusu), o for a (lobs)
obstruent clusters take the voicing of their last member, as in Latvian (lobs with [ps], vuords with [ts])
/v/ is a glide [u̯] at the end of a syllable after a vowel
vowels are fronted next to palatalised consonants and retracted next to plain ones; [ɨ] and [i], and the diphthongs yu and iu, alternate accordingly
/r/ is an alveolar trill; /x f/ occur in loanwords
phonotactics: syllable tones only on long syllables (long vowel, diphthong, or short vowel plus sonorant)
y only after plain consonants, i only after palatalised consonants or word-initially
final consonant clusters with -s are common (vuords, bolss, cylvāks)

stress.rule: Stress falls on the first syllable, with a few exceptions of the same kind as in Latvian.
stress.cues: intensity and pitch; length and tone are independent of stress

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none in careful speech; short final vowels are weakened or lost in many varieties
rhythm.notes: The class label is an impression from the descriptive literature; no rhythm-metric study is cited.

length.notes: Vowel length is phonemic. No published duration figures for Latgalian are quoted here.

intonation.declarative: highest pitch on the stressed first syllable of the prominent word, fall to a low ending
intonation.yes_no_question: rise on the last stressed syllable or at the end of the phrase; a question particle may introduce the question
intonation.wh_question: high on the question word, then falling
intonation.continuation: rise or high level at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: high or falling pitch beginning on the stressed initial syllable
intonation.notes: I know of no instrumental study of Latgalian intonation; this follows the general Latvian pattern and has low confidence.

tone.tone_bearing_unit: syllable (long syllables only; clearest in the stressed syllable)

inventory.name: falling tone
inventory.description: pitch and intensity fall through the long syllable; corresponds to both the level and the falling tone of Central Latvian

inventory.name: broken tone
inventory.description: pitch rises in the first part of the syllable, is interrupted by a glottal closure or creak, and the short second part is lower and weaker
inventory.phonation: glottal stop or creaky voice in the middle of the syllable
inventory.duration: long, with a short second part

tone.notes: Chao numerals are a schematic rendering of the descriptions of the High Latvian two-tone system (Nau 2011; Balode & Holvoet 2001; Laua 1997 for the tone shapes), not measured values. The tones are not written and their functional load is low.

phonation: glottalisation (glottal stop or creak) inside syllables with the broken tone

problems: There is little Latgalian of its own: the voice uses the Latvian phoneme table and the Latvian dictionary (phonemes lv, dictionary lv) with three conditional rules (dictrules 2): o is short [o], ō is [uo], and no break is inserted after y before a vowel.
No palatalisation: consonants before front vowels and soft final consonants are read as plain Latvian consonants (dīna, sirds, saceit, byut); only ļ, ņ, ķ, ģ are palatal.
No syllable tones and no glottalisation for the broken tone.
The diphthong yu is two separate vowels (myusu has three syllables).
Narrow or wide e is chosen by the rules written for Latvian words.
No regressive voicing assimilation (lobs, vuords, golds keep [bs], [ds]).
o in words that the Latvian rules treat as loanwords is still long [oː] (školā).
y is shown as 'y' in IPA output although the sound is [ɨ].
Only the default eSpeak tunes are used; wh-questions get the same fall-rise as yes-no questions.
good: initial stress and phonemic vowel length
short [o] for the letter o (Latgola, lobs, golds) and [uo] for uo and ō
diphthongs ie, uo, ai, ei, au, iu as single phonemes
own pitch range and stress settings in the voice file

notes: The consonant and vowel inventories follow Nau (2011) in outline; descriptions differ on how far the soft series extends (labials, postalveolars) and on the status of /ɨ/ as a phoneme or as the allophone of /i/ after plain consonants. No formant, VOT or rhythm-metric values are given because I know of no published figures for Latgalian.
